Title: Case Study: Player withdrawing from the game

Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
Hello All,

One of the most disruptive events in a game is when a player must
leave in the middle. It's also an incredibly hard situation to
judge. The benefit of case studies is that everyone can share their
ideas, and hopefully reach consensus.

5 player game. A->B->C->D->E

Everyone takes their first turn. D brings up a 4-cap, no one else
brings out anyone, nor discards.
On his second turn, B brings up a 3-cap. Still no discard.
On D's second turn, D plays a clan-specific master card. Then, C gets
a phone call and immediately announces, "I need to go - I'm really
sorry."

Assuming you don't have a substitute for C (which is pretty much
always the best option), what do you about the table above?

If you want/need any other clarifying information about this
situation, feel free to ask (and perhaps mention why it would make a
difference in your final ruling.)

LSJ, I'd love it if you posted your answer, too!

Ira

If this were a chess game, the answer would be simple. Not only would
the defaulting player automatically lose, but his opponent would
automatically win.

Here, nobody would have a problem with the idea that "C" should
automatically lose. However, since there are 4 other players, perhaps
it is unclear who, if anyone, should receive the corresponding "win".

In theory, there is a simple answer. The rules say that when a player
loses, he loses to his predator. By simple analogy, one could rule
that when a player defaults, he defaults to his predator. One might
apply this simple solution by removing "D"s cards and counters from
the table, giving "C" a victory point, and simply continuing the
game. Since no "oust" occurred, there seems no reason to give "C" a 6-
pool reward, however.

Some folks might argue this unfair to the other players, and possibly
a collusion hazard.

An alternative might be to create a system that delays the reward and
gives it an opportunity to pass around the table. Here's an example
off the top of my head:

When the defaulting player leaves, place a "default card" in front of
the defaulting player's predator, with a number of "default counters"
equal to the defaulting player's last pool total. Play now continues
normally, among the remaining players, except that during his untap
phase, the player with the "default card" burns 2 default counter from
the card, and burns an additional 2 counters from the card if his prey
loses any pool during his minion phase. If the player with the
default card is ousted, his predator gains control of the default
card. When the default card has no more counters, it is burned, and
the player who had the card when it burned gains a victory point.

far more reasonable than having the judge devise a new solution each

I think a number of different systems could be devised. But the

But the situations are going to be different every time, and no single,
universally applied situation is going to remotely work for different
situations. Assume Player C, for whatever reason, needs to abruptly
leave the game in the following games:

Game 1: It is a 5 players game, everyone has taken 1 turn, no one has
influenced out anyone.

Game 2: It is a 5 player game, it is turn 10, Player A is ousted, Player
C (the one leaving) is at 4 pool and has 1 tapped, bloodless minion in
play.

Game 3: It is a 4 player game, it is turn 4, everyone has some minions
in play, folks have taken some actions, nothing significant has
happened, but it is way too late to just remove someone and move on.

No blanket solution will address all of these situations, even remotely.
As a judge, I'd say that Game 1 just moves on from there as a 4 player
game, adjusting transfers as necessary; Game 2 just continues as a 5
player game with player C being represented by the number 4; Game 3
needs to have someone sit in as player C if at all possible.

> I think a number of different systems could be devised. But the
> starting assumption should be that, not only does the defaulting
> player lose the victory point he brought with him to the table, but he
> leaves it behind at the table so that it will be given, sooner or
> later, to one of the remaining players, or perhaps divided between
> them.

That isn't going to be necessarily appropriate in all situations. It is
unfortunate if a 5 player game needs to become a 4 player game, but the
same thing happens when someone drops between rounds (i.e. a 20 player
tournament suddenly becomes a 19 player tournament after the first
round). And I don't think that this is a common enough circumstance that
there needs to be a mandated solution--in, what, 10+ years of
competitive VTES play, I can't remember a single time when someone had
to leave *in the middle* of a game--people drop between rounds. And at
least a few times, someone just didn't show up for the start of a round
after they had been seated. But getting a call in the middle of a game
and suddenly up and leaving due to an emergency? I can't remember a
single time that I have seen this happen in a tournament I have been
involved in. Such that I suspect it really doesn't happen all that often.

When the defaulting player leaves, place a "default sheet" in front of
the defaulting player's predator with the defaulting player's last
pool total written on it. Play now continues normally, among the

remaining players, except that during his untap phase, the player with

the "default sheet" adds 1 "default counter" to the sheet, and adds an
additional 1 default counter to the sheet at the end of his turn if
his prey loses any pool during that turn. If the player with the
default card is ousted or withdraws, his predator gains control of the
default card. When the default card has counters greater than or
equal to half the pool total written on it, it is burned, and the
player who had the card when it burned gains one victory point and
gains pool equal to 6 minus the number of default counters on the card
(but never loses pool). The player who controls the card at the end
of the game gains a half victory point.

> happened, but it is way too late to just remove someone and move on.

Place however a default sheet with (probably) about "15" written on it
in front of player B, and continue as indicated above.

could be improved some, does seem to address all these situations, at
least remotely.

player, I don't see why that cannot be done. Rules can be bent if all
consent. But rules are for when there is disagreement, and, it
seems to me that once a game has begun, it has begun. If such a
system is devised, then it seems to me that a separate rule for such
situations is not worth the remote chance that such timing will occur

If the defaulting player's deck remains available, and if a
replacement player is available, perhaps having a replacement player
sit in (without, I think, being allowed to familiarize himself with
the deck) should ALWAYS be the preferred solution. Perhaps this
preference should be part of the single comprehensive system (at the
risk of making it more complex).

I note that this solution (when it is an option) also has the benefit
I value, but that you scoff at, of preserving for the table the
victory point that the defaulting player brought to the table.

The idea is not that all situations should be treated the same (my
system does not do that) but rather there should be a single
comprehensive system that always tells the judge how to deal with the
situation.

If the judge makes things up as he goes along, then no-one, even the
judge, can ever be sure how his judgment has been influenced. He may
formulate a solution that helps someone he likes, or screws someone he
dislikes. He may overcompensate and formulate a solution that helps
someone he dislikes, and screws someone he likes. Perceptions of
unfair favoritism -- even when unjustified -- can be created by those
who disagree with the appropriateness of the solution. Even where the
judge does his best to be fair, an appearance of impropriety can be
created, along with resentment.

If the solution is decided in advance, by a single set of rules that
always tells the judge how to act, then such problems can be
avoided. If people are dissatisfied, they will blame the rules, not
the judge, and bad feelings will tend to be avoided.

I believe that the current system is pretty good. My issue with the
current system is that there are multiple correct answers given the
same input. In the fairly simple case I described (C must leave on
turn 2.4), these answers were all proposed:

a) Do nothing, play on.
b) Remove one of D's upcoming transfers
c) Rewind to the beginning of the game

If I were the judge, and I ruled (a), I would be correct. If LSJ were
the judge and he ruled (b), he would be equally correct. And if David
Tatu were the judge, and he ruled (c), he would be equally correct,
too. We would all be correct by definition: we're the judge, and we
use our judgement.

I believe we can improve our current system if judges make similar
rulings given the same input. I believe that consistency across
judges can be achieved through Case Studies, followed by discussion
and hopefully consensus. LSJ helpfully posted his thoughts on this
Case Study. I hope all future judges, when encountering a similar
situation, will be able to refer to this discussion.

B is at 1 pool, no ready minions, will surely die next turn, and has
no hope to oust C. C has 3 pool, but good defenses with intercept,
bounce, votes, etc, and regular poolgain each turn with blood dolls,
hunting grounds, etc. On B's turn, C gets a phone call and needs to
leave immediately.

> ever was one.

There are many complex fields of study that are taught partially
through Case Studies, and they've been shown to be an effective
teaching tool. One of the most common ways to teach Ethics, which
requires judgement of multiple shades of gray, is through Case
Studies.

Of course, if Peter and nystulc just want to flame back and forth all
day, I agree that it becomes less useful. :)

> Oh, my, it seems painfully obvious you cannot. Or rather, perhaps you
> could but the cross-section of discussed cases would always be so small
> as to be fairly worthless as a tool for future judging.

I disagree. From my experience, the same sorts of challenges come up
over and over while judging tournaments. There are always variations
on a theme. Sure, you won't have *exactly* the same input conditions,
but humans are excellent at identifying patterns and extrapolating
related answers.

> the "consensus" might actually be counter-productive because of the
> temptation to use some temptingly similar discussed case as a baseline
> only to discover a few specific details can make a lot of difference in
> reckoning "fairness".

I disagree. Spending time thinking about complicated, multi-faceted
judging situations can only help to make a judge more aware of all the
issues when making a future judgement.

Thinking about things from multiple different perspectives,
considering all the options, is a skill that can be improved and honed
with practice. Case Studies are an opportunity for such a practice.

Also, and I didn't mention this before, Case Studies are an
opportunity to identify any outliers. If someone responds to a Case
Study with an obviously-bad solution, it's useful for the community to
give them feedback and an opportunity to reassess their judgement for
that case. So not only do Case Studies help hone in on the several
good solutions, they also help rule out the obviously bad solutions.

you've stated.) Use your guidelines - I support them, and I think

the guidelines give you a result that's unfair or doesn't actually
keep the balance.
